{{Short description|Algebraic structure}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''G''-module}}
[[File:Toroidal coord.png|thumb|The [[torus]] can be made an abelian group isomorphic to the product of the [[circle group]]. This abelian group is a [[Klein four-group]]-module, where the group acts by reflection in each of the coordinate directions (here depicted by red and blue arrows intersecting at the identity element).]]

In [[mathematics]], given a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math>, a '''''G''-module''' is an [[abelian group]] <math>M</math> on which <math>G</math> [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] compatibly with the abelian group structure on <math>M</math>. This widely applicable notion generalizes that of a [[group representation|representation of {{math|''G''}}]]. [[Group cohomology|Group (co)homology]] provides an important set of tools for studying general <math>G</math>-modules.

The term '''''G''-module''' is also used for the more general notion of an [[module (mathematics)|{{math|''R''}}-module]] on which <math>G</math> acts linearly (i.e. as a group of <math>R</math>-module [[automorphism]]s).

==Definition and basics==
Let <math>G</math> be a group. A '''left <math>G</math>-module''' consists of<ref>{{cite book |title=Representation Theory of Finite Groups and Associative Algebras |year=1988 |first1=Charles W. |last1=Curtis |first2=Irving |last2=Reiner |author1-link=Charles W. Curtis |author2-link=Irving Reiner |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |orig-year=1962 |isbn=978-0-470-18975-7 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/representationth11curt}}<!---citation template accepts only one isbn---(ISBN 978-0821840665)---></ref> an abelian group <math>M</math> together with a [[Group action (mathematics)|left group action]] <math>\rho:G\times M\to M</math> such that
:<math>g\cdot(a_1+a_2)=g\cdot a_1+g\cdot a_2</math>
for all <math>a_1</math> and <math>a_2</math> in <math>M</math> and all <math>g</math> in <math>G</math>, where <math>g\cdot a</math> denotes <math>\rho(g,a)</math>. A '''right <math>G</math>-module''' is defined similarly. Given a left <math>G</math>-module <math>M</math>, it can be turned into a right <math>G</math>-module by defining <math>a\cdot g=g^{-1}\cdot a</math>.

A [[function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f:M\rightarrow N</math> is called a '''morphism of <math>G</math>-modules''' (or a '''<math>G</math>-linear map''', or a '''<math>G</math>-homomorphism''') if <math>f</math> is both a [[group homomorphism]] and <math>G</math>-[[equivariant]].

The collection of left (respectively right) <math>G</math>-modules and their morphisms form an [[abelian category]] <math>G\textbf{-Mod}</math> (resp. <math>\textbf{Mod-}G</math>). The category <math>G\text{-Mod}</math> (resp. <math>\text{Mod-}G</math>) can be identified with the category of left (resp. right) '''<math>\mathbb{Z}G</math>-modules''', i.e. with the [[module (mathematics)|modules]] over the [[group ring]] <math>\mathbb{Z}[G]</math>.

A '''submodule''' of a <math>G</math>-module <math>M</math> is a subgroup <math>A\subseteq M</math> that is stable under the action of <math>G</math>, i.e. <math>g\cdot a\in A</math> for all <math>g\in G</math> and <math>a\in A</math>. Given a submodule <math>A</math> of <math>M</math>, the '''quotient module''' <math>M/A</math> is the [[quotient group]] with action <math>g\cdot (m+A)=g\cdot m+A</math>.

==Examples==
*Given a group <math>G</math>, the abelian group <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is a <math>G</math>-module with the ''trivial action'' <math>g\cdot a=a</math>.
*Let <math>M</math> be the set of [[binary quadratic form]]s <math>f(x,y)=ax^2+2bxy+cy^2</math> with <math>a,b,c</math> [[integer]]s, and let <math>G=\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})</math> (the 2×2 [[special linear group]] over <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>). Define
::<math>(g\cdot f)(x,y)=f((x,y)g^t)=f\left((x,y)\cdot\begin{bmatrix}
     \alpha & \gamma \\
     \beta & \delta
  \end{bmatrix}\right)=f(\alpha x+\beta y,\gamma x+\delta y),</math>
:where
::<math>g=\begin{bmatrix}
     \alpha & \beta \\
     \gamma & \delta
  \end{bmatrix}</math>
:and <math>(x,y)g</math> is [[matrix multiplication]]. Then <math>M</math> is a <math>G</math>-module studied by [[Gauss]].<ref>{{Citation| title= Integral Quadratic Forms and Lattices: Proceedings of the International Conference on Integral Quadratic Forms and Lattices, June 15–19, 1998, Seoul National University, Korea|first1=Myung-Hwan |last1= Kim |publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|year=1999}}</ref> Indeed, we have

:: <math>g(h(f(x,y))) = gf((x,y)h^t)=f((x,y)h^tg^t)=f((x,y)(gh)^t)=(gh)f(x,y).</math>

*If <math>V</math> is a representation of <math>G</math> over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>K</math>, then <math>V</math> is a <math>G</math>-module (it is an abelian group under addition).

==Topological groups==
If <math>G</math> is a [[topological group]] and <math>M</math> is an abelian topological group, then a '''topological ''G''-module''' is a <math>G</math>-module where the action map <math>G\times M\rightarrow M</math> is [[continuous function|continuous]] (where the [[product topology]] is taken on <math>G\times M</math>).<ref>{{cite journal| title= Algebraic cohomology of topological groups| author=D. Wigner| journal= Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.| volume=178 |year=1973|pages=83–93| doi=10.1090/s0002-9947-1973-0338132-7| doi-access=free}}</ref>

In other words, a topological <math>G</math>-module is an abelian topological group <math>M</math> together with a continuous map <math>G\times M\rightarrow M</math> satisfying the usual relations <math>g(a+a')=ga+ga'</math>, <math>(gg')a=g(g'a)</math>, and <math>1a=a</math>.
